sections.heading: ABSTRACT
sections.text: This study explores transdisciplinary knowledge creation through commun­ ities of practice (CoPs) to enhance boundary crossings. Research on CoPs is yet to focus on people with no concern or interest in CoPs, who are ignored as “outsiders.” However, these individuals could be candidates for the future and involving them and using their knowledge would be effective for solving complex social problems. We review transdisciplinary research and argue for the usefulness of building transdisciplinary communities of practice (TDCoPs) to enhance boundary crossings and involve disinterested people. Furthermore, transformative boundary objects (TBOs) are effective in promot­ ing learning that alters stereotypes and prejudices (transformative learning). We conducted case studies focusing on “municipal meister” institutions in Japan. We searched for 22 municipalities in which such institutions existed and selected four successful municipalities to build case studies. All the cases built CoPs to improve knowledge transfer and attempted to involve local res­ idents and craftspeople in their events. We also discuss the identification of successful points in building TDCoPs, how to develop CoPs for TDCoPs, and how to use TBOs. This study contributes to the theory of CoPs and boundary objects, and suggests practical implications for learning and other purposes, such as the grand challenge. KEYWORDS Communities of practice; transdisciplinary research; transdisciplinary commun­ ities of practice; transformative boundary objects; municipal meister

sections.heading: Introduction
sections.text: This study explored the use of transdisciplinary knowledge creation through communities of practice (CoPs) to enhance boundary crossing. The success and failure of CoPs was examined by focusing on “municipal meister” institutions in Japan. We discuss how to involve people as CoP members by improving boundary crossing, especially for those who have no concerns or interests, such as disinter­ ested people. These people have been ignored in previous research as “outsiders” to CoPs (Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder 2002 ). They are potential members, so we should discuss how to involve them, which could contribute to the development of CoP research and complex problem-solving. CoP research can be classified as three research topic categories or lens (Nicolini et al. 2022 ): learning lens (Beane 2019 ; Pyrko, D € orfler, and Eden 2019 ), innovation lens (Kirkman et al. 2013 ; Swan, Scarbrough, and Robertson 2002 ), and defending lens (Hong and O 2009 ; Mørk et al. 2010 ). Several studies argue that CoPs can form a collaboration comprising people with similar interests (Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder 2002 ) and help them interact (Wenger 1998 ), while facilitating knowledge creation (Iedema, Meyerkort, and White 2005 ), transfer (Bechky 2003 ; Moodysson 2008 ), storage (Marshall, Shipman, and McCall 1995 ), combination (Buckley and Carter 2004 ), and sharing (Barley and Kunda 2001 ; Nicholls and Cargill 2008 ). Furthermore, CoPs enhance boundary crossing (Engestr € om 2016 ) by building an accumulating structure namely the “double-knitted structure” (Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder 2002 ) between the organization and CoPs or a multi-layered structure between CoPs (Matsumoto 2024 ), which facilitates learning (Wenger 1998 ) and problem-solving (Swan, Scarbrough, and Robertson 2002 ) and innovation (Ernst and Chrobot-Mason 2011 ). Recent societal problems such as global warming, climate change, and environmental protec­ tion have become complex. Such problems form the grand challenge aspect, and tackling these difficult social problems is important (Whittington and Yakis-Douglas 2020 ). However, to solve such problems, it is essential to collaborate with different stakeholders, such as academic researchers, businesspeople, public officials, and the general public (Ackermann, Pyrko, and Hill 2023 ; Matsumoto, Kasamatsu, and Sakakibara 2022 ). Transdisciplinary communities of practice involving these stakeholders (Cundill, Roux, and Parker 2015 ) or interactive groups (Wenger- Trayner and Wenger-Trayner 2020 , 2021 ) have an effect on addressing this grand challenge. To generate the knowledge necessary to solve complex social problems, the participation of various multidisciplinary and transdisciplinary stakeholders should be secured (Tress, Tress, and Fry 2006 ). This requires both academic scholars and nonacademic participants. Nurturing CoPs has proven to be effective in enhancing boundary-crossing participation (Cundill, Roux, and Parker 2015 ; Matsumoto, Kasamatsu, and Sakakibara 2022 ). Such communities are efficient in forming a collaboration of participants who share similar interests for common purposes (Matsumoto 2018 ; Silverstein et al. 2022 ; Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder 2002 ). However, previous research has not considered how CoPs engage “disinterested people” who do not share concerns or interests. Members are assumed to be interested in participating in CoPs. In the well-known definition of a CoP (Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder 2002 , 4), mem­ bers are assumed to share concerns about an issue. Concern and interest are essential for com­ munities ((MacIver 1924 ) and CoPs (Corso, Giacobbe, and Martini 2009 ) and motivate members to interact (Zboralski 2009 ) and participate (Victor and Hendrix 2014 ). These people have been ignored as “outsiders” to CoPs (Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder 2002 ), but is also true that they may become members in the future. Similarly, it is necessary to stimulate interest in CoPs to increase membership across disciplin­ ary boundaries. However, the increase in boundary-crossing participation among those who do not share an identified interest remains unclear. Building transdisciplinary CoPs among stake­ holders is essential. However, previous studies have not considered this problem. On the other hand, collaborative learning and boundary crossing are critical to firms’ sustainable growth (Ernst and Chrobot-Mason 2011 ; Lesser and Storck 2001 ). CoPs can contribute to organiza­ tions by enhancing knowledge sharing (Anand, Gardner, and Morris 2007 ; Wasko and Faraj 2005 ), developing social capital (Dutta and Rangnekar 2022 ; Lesser and Storck 2001 ) and building know­ ledge resources (von Krogh 2002 ). Similarly, collaborative learning between different stakeholders is useful

Our study can contribute to CoP research in four ways. First, we can clarify how to build CoPs transdisciplinar­ ily. Previous research has discussed this (Cundill, Roux, and Parker 2015 ), but is still abstract. Our case study is useful for discussing concretize methods, both theoretically and practically. Second, we highlighted the importance of applying transdisciplinary research (TDR) to manage­ ment theory. Previous research has suggested the importance of tackling complex social problems, such as grand challenges (George et al. 2016 ), but meaningful discussions from the TDR perspec­ tive of environmental and sustainability research are still scarce (Tress et al. 2006 ). We believe that TDRs have many useful implications for management theories; therefore, we demonstrate their importance by discussing our case from a TDR perspective. Third, we suggest how to involve different stakeholders and other people in solving problems by discussing how to involve “disinterested people.” CoP research deals with members who have concerns and interests (Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder 2002 ), but to solve complex problems, we need to involve many people from different disciplines and perspectives (Lang et al. 2012 ). In our cases, many people who were not initially concerned gradually participated in their CoPs, acquired knowledge, and built mutual connections. This may have implications on the involvement of various individ­ uals. Fourth, we discovered a method to promote transformative learning, which is learning that changes people’s values or perspectives by discussing transformative boundary objects (TBOs). To enhance the participation of disinterested people, it is important to learn the meaning of CoPs’ activities (Matsumoto, Kasamatsu, and Sakakibara 2022 ). TBOs could be useful in proceeding with learning that changes thinking, which is important for CoP research to discuss how to pro­ ceed with more members. Our research has practical implications for training employees in companies. As in other coun­ tries, collaborative learning in organizations influences competitive advantage in Japan (Kambayashi 2015 ; Kuriyama 2017 ). However, employee training still depends on the company, making it difficult for individuals to learn their skills autonomously. Encouraging spontaneous learning is a critical issue in Japan as a whole and in other countries, so the case of the municipal meister’s institutions used in this study can contribute to solving such problems. Moreover, the transdisciplinary view influences the business environment of Japanese companies and the prob­ lem-solving of Japanese employees. They generally understand the importance of Nonaka and Takeuchi ( 1995 ) knowledge creation theory, and learn more about transdisciplinary perspectives, especially for their sustainable activities in the global environment. This study contributes to the literature on these aspects.

sections.heading: Boundary crossing and CoPs
sections.text: Boundary crossing–moving across boundaries horizontally and vertically (Engestr € om 2016 )—facil­ itates knowledge creation between teams (Faraj and Yan 2009 ), organizations (Engestr € om 2016 ), and companies (Ernst and Chrobot-Mason 2011 ). Through boundary crossing, organizations can increase personnel diversity (Nonaka and Takeuchi 1995 ), obtain various resources (Faraj and Yan 2009 ), and share information (Kelly 2004 ). These measures can greatly enhance problem solving (Swan, Scarbrough, and Robertson 2002 ), innovation (Ernst and Chrobot-Mason 2011 ), and learning (Wenger 1998 ). Therefore, it is important to implement and enhance the boundary crossing. Boundary crossing can be achieved by nurturing CoPs, which are defined as “groups of people who share a concern, a set of problems or passion about a topic, and who deepen their know­ ledge and expertise in this area by interacting on an ongoing basis” (Wenger, McDermott, and 28

sections.text: Snyder 2002 , 4). CoPs promote learning and innovation (Nicolini et al. 2022 ). Learning occurs by facilitating the transfer of skills among members (Lave and Wenger 1991 ), promoting the creation and sharing of knowledge (Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder 2002 ), encouraging members to engage in practice (Wenger 1998 ), and supporting the development of their identities (Wenger- Trayner and Wenger-Trayner 2020 ). Another effective way to enhance learning is to cross the boundaries between the organization and the CoP. CoPs enable boundary crossings between organizations by building “double-knitted structures” (Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder 2002 , 18). Specifically, CoPs allow employees to cross various organizational boundaries between groups (Ben-Menahem et al. 2016 ), within a hierarchy (Bogenrieder and Nooteboom 2004 ), across departments (Bechky 2003 ), and among branches, enterprises, and countries (Dewhurst and Cegarra Navarro 2004 ). These crossings facilitate knowledge creation (Jørgensen and Lauridsen 2005 ) and sharing (Buckley and Carter 2004 ). This study focused on boundary crossing to consider ways to improve learning. Compared to other methods, boundary crossing is related to learning in the future as well as at present. Gathering members is important for CoPs; this involves not just waiting for them to arrive. Involving through boundary spanner (Ernst and Chrobot-Mason 2011 ) or broker (Ishiyama 2016 ; Wenger 1998 ) using boundary object (Carlile 2002 ), managing boundary work (Faraj and Yan 2009 ) are effective, but as we claim in next subsection, considering “disinterested people” is vital to discussing a suitable way of boundary crossing that improves and continues learning.

sections.heading: The “disinterested people” outside the CoP
sections.text: Considering the issues of CoPs and boundary crossing, it is useful to focus on interest, as it is the source of all social activities (MacIver 1924 ). Interest in the domain, community, and practice is a key factor in building a CoP (Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder 2002 ). Interests that form communities and associations can be divided into two categories: interest in relationships, and interest in knowledge and skills (MacIver 1924 ). This classification is also valid for CoPs and can be specified based on the interests of the community and the domain. Participation in a CoP is facilitated by one or both these interests. Conversely, “disinterested people” outside the CoP have been ignored in CoP research (Matsumoto, Kasamatsu, and Sakakibara 2022 ). Members of a CoP are categorized as core, active, peripheral, or outsiders based on their degree of willingness to participate (Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder 2002 ). Outsiders are described as those located near CoP boundaries. Given that per­ ipheral members participate modestly within the boundaries of the CoP, outsiders are interested in the practices of the CoP, but have not yet participated. Outsiders and “disinterested people,” therefore, differ in their meanings. The three practices for boundary crossing proposed by Wenger ( 1998 )—namely, boundary practice, overlapping, and peripherality—do not consider “disinterested people.” In the past, disinterested people were neglected in CoP research because the concept was used to promote learning and knowledge creation through autonomous interactions with interested people. However, bringing disinterested people into a CoP may be a key factor in resolving vari­ ous problems. Some studies have offered useful suggestions regarding this issue. The first suggestion is to research the boundary work in team management. Boundary-spanning behavior increases the psychological safety of members (Faraj and Yan 2009 ) and promotes community and trust build­ ing (Ernst and Chrobot-Mason 2011 ). Although these studies advocate for the importance of managing team boundaries, they target team members and do not consider disinterested parties. The second suggestion is conducting business ecosystem research. By understanding the connec­ tions among stakeholders as part of an ecosystem, it is possible to understand system innovation

However, this is a firm-level theory and individuals are considered members of the stakeholder group. The third suggestion is conducting research on the landscape of practice (LoP). This con­ cept, proposed by Wenger-Trayner ( 2013 ) and Wenger-Trayner et al. ( 2014 ), is intended to cross the boundaries between CoPs (Pyrko, D € orfler, and Eden 2019 ). The LoP is perceived as a broader concept that includes the linkages among CoPs and the interconnection of practices and know­ ledge. Wenger-Trayner ( 2013 ) argued that this facilitates mutual border crossing and that all practices, including encounters and conflicts, lead to learning. Thus, the LoP promotes loose col­ laboration (Pyrko, D € orfler, and Eden 2019 ) and capacity building (Wenger-Trayner 2013 ) among CoPs. Although such inclusive concepts have been explored at the CoP level (Love 2009 ; Matsumoto 2018 ), LoP builds on and develops the CoP theory. However, mechanisms for engag­ ing disinterested populations outside CoPs have not yet been considered.

sections.heading: Transdisciplinarity and CoPs
sections.text: This study addresses the question of how to involve disinterested people in CoP. Transdisciplinary research (TDR) has been used to address this issue. This paradigm shift is required to solve the vexing problem of sustainability research (OECD 2020 ). TDR advocates the importance of involving disinterested people and using these research findings to support trans­ disciplinarity can provide useful results. Transdisciplinarity concerns what is at once between, across, and beyond all disciplines (Nicolescu 2014 ). Management studies have highlighted the importance of multidisciplinary (e.g., Ferlie et al. 2005 ; Ben-Menahem et al. 2016 ) and business ecosystem studies (e.g., Ihrig and MacMillan 2017 ). This difference lies in the inclusion of nonacademic participants, even those who do not share similar interests (Tress, Tress, and Fry 2006 ), which is important for solving social problems related to various stakeholders (Jahn, Bergmann, and Keil 2012 ; Lang et al. 2012 ). TDR has been defined as a partnership among participants within and outside academia that transcends disciplinary barriers and fields, and involves those who are most affected by the prob­ lems to be addressed (Belcher et al. 2016 ; Lang et al. 2012 ). In other words, TDR is context- specific, problem-oriented research that crosses disciplinary and institutional boundaries (Carew and Wickson 2010 ). TDR is characterized by interaction and collaboration across disciplinary boundaries. However, as Tress, Tress, and Fry ( 2006 ) showed, TDR differs between participatory and interdisciplinary research ( Figure 1 ). Tress, Tress, and Fry ( 2006 ) summarized four types of research on the axes of participation and nonparticipation of nonacademic participants and the integration of disciplinary knowledge, as presented in Figure 2 . Transdisciplinary CoPs require two practices: the participation of nona­ cademic participants and the integration of knowledge among different disciplines. Even when TDR is pursued, numerous obstacles must be overcome before it can be real­ ized. Overcoming the challenge of collaborating with community residents and other nonaca­ demic participants is also problematic (Mobj € ork 2010 ). An important aspect of TDR is the co-creation of knowledge (Steelman et al. 2021 ). In addition to collaboration among research­ ers from different academic fields (L � el � e and Norgaard 2005 ), collaboration between societal stakeholders and researchers is also crucial (De Jong et al. 2011 ; Polk 2015 ). This study thus focuses on two concepts of sustainability research that are useful in addressing this issue: transdisciplinary communities of practice (TDCoPs) and transformative boundary objects (TBOs). 30

sections.heading: Transdisciplinary CoPs
sections.text: Cundill, Roux, and Parker ( 2015 ) proposed the creation of TDCoPs. They explained the concept of TDCoP as “more likely to be distinctly heterogeneous, cross-sectoral groups with a shared interest in and a basic commitment to solving complex social-ecological problems” and “to copro­ duce knowledge for practical application and solutions to current challenges.” TDCoPs can be valuable in pursuing multidisciplinary scientific insights from scientists, as well as including nona­ cademic stakeholders such as companies, policymakers, and citizens in collaboration to resolve complex social problems. Consequently, TDCoP enhances boundary crossing among participants from different perspectives. Matsumoto, Kasamatsu, and Sakakibara ( 2022 ) note that one obstacle to problem solving using TDCoPs is attracting the interest of local populations. Involving them in a TDCoP enables knowledge creation and continuous problem solving from a field perspective. Cundill, Roux, and Parker ( 2015 ) also offered suggestions on how to nurture TDCoPs and outlined three crucial lessons: (1) opportunities must be purposefully created for outsiders to observe activities in the core group; (2) CoPs cannot be artificially created, but they can be Figure 1. Therefore, this study examines the formation process of TDCoPs, during which the key factor for ensuring the success of their activities is understanding how to involve disinterested people in the problem to be solved. TBOs have been proposed to overcome this problem.

sections.heading: Transformative boundary objects
sections.text: Boundary objects (BOs) have been employed since the early stages to promote collaboration and knowledge creation within CoPs (Wenger 1998 ). BOs include artifacts, documents, vocabulary, and concepts that connect people across physical, academic, and relational boundaries. This con­ cept was originally introduced by Star and Griesemer ( 1989 ) and applied to the context of CoPs by Wenger ( 1998 ). BOs promote boundary crossings and interactions between CoP members and those around them (Wenger 1998 ), which are also important in sustainability research (Simon and Schiemer 2015 ). BOs also promote communication across boundaries between actor groups (Lundgren 2021 ), promote collaboration among stakeholders with conflicting perspectives (Steger et al. 2021 ), arouse interest, and encourage boundary crossing (White, Larson, and Wutich 2018 ). The concept of TBOs (Sakakibara et al. 2019 ) introduced in this study was originally proposed by Tsurusaki et al. ( 2013 ) in education. TBOs not only connect people across the world—the ori­ ginal function of BO—but also provide opportunities to transform the perceptions and values of disinterested people. TBOs differ from BOs in their relationships with diverse stakeholders, and are closely connected to the problems to be addressed. In the process of connecting people, TBOs foster transformative learning among participants after TDCoPs are formed, by prompting inter­ actions and collaboration among stakeholders. In contrast to acquiring knowledge and informa­ tion, transformative learning involves fundamental changes in learners’ values, preconceptions, beliefs (Argyris and Sch € on 1978 ; Fiol and Lyles 1985 ), frames of reference, and meaningful per­ spectives (Mezirow 1991 ; Sato, Pemba, and Nakagawa 2018 ). Although the community residents were aware of conservation problems, they were not inter­ ested in addressing these issues. “Environmental icons”—wildlife or ecosystems emblematic of connections with nature—serve as shared cultural values, and function as TBOs to arouse interest and catalyze action, thereby promoting participation among community residents. Matsumoto ( 2018 ) noted that videos focusing on dementia-related problems can function as TBOs that facili­ tate the formation of CoPs for the treatment of dementia that cross local boundaries. The forma­ tion of TDCoPs involving disinterested users through TBOs is essential.

sections.heading: Case studies: Theoretical framework and presenting problems
sections.text: We consider the theoretical framework for this case study. Building TDCoPs is effective for involving people from outside who do not have an interest in the activity or problem solving. Transdisciplinary research claims that bringing together people from different disciplines is more effective in tackling complex problems. However, to involve these people as members of TDCoPs, it is necessary to allow them to cross boundaries and participate in learning activities. The key to promoting boundary crossing is twofold: building and managing TDCoPs to promote the bound­ ary crossing of disinterested people and using TBOs to promote transformative learning to change participants’ values and perspectives. We summarize the problems discussed in the following sections using case studies. For effect­ ive learning and interaction in CoPs, we need to bring together not only members who have con­ cerns and interests, but also those who do not. Disinterested people who do not yet have concerns or interests can be considered candidates for CoPs in the future and should be encour­ aged to cross boundaries and be involved in sustainable activities. However, previous studies have 32

sections.text: ignored these people as “outsiders” and have not considered effective ways of involving them. In the previous sections, we discussed this problem by reviewing the TDR on knowledge creation and problem solving involving different stakeholders. From the existing studies, we found the importance of building transdisciplinary communities of practice (TDCoP). However, there has been little research on TDCoP, and an effective method to build TDCoP remains unclear. The following section addresses this issue. How can a TDCoP be constructed effectively? What is important? Likewise, we also found that using a Transformational Boundary Object (TBO) is an useful alternative for involving disinterested people by conducting transformative learning. A TBO can transform people’s stereotypes and prejudices in transformative learning, making them interested in improving boundary crossing for participating CoPs. However, only a few studies have been conducted on TBOs, and these theories remain under construction. In this study, we address this problem. What is a TBO? How can this approach be applied to transformative learning? Previous studies have not addressed these issues. Most research discusses the gathering of members for problem-solving but lacks a transdisciplinary view. CoP research investigated how to gather members, but ignored “disinterested people” as outsiders. Moreover, much of the research on boundary crossing considered moving people but did not imagine the change in their values and perspectives. We address these problems or gaps in the structuring methods of TDCoPs to improve complex problem-solving. To address these issues, case studies have been conducted on “municipal meister institutions.”

sections.heading: Research site
sections.text: We adopted a qualitative research method and constructed four case studies of municipal meister institutions as transdisciplinary CoPs. In order to use, compare, and reflect on these cases, we addressed our research question of how CoP facilitates transdisciplinary boundary crossing among different participants, including “disinterested people.” These institutions in Japan are unique, although there are many similar institutions across the country. Given the unique nature of meister institutions, we conducted a comparative analysis between them and other similar institutions. To select the research site, we considered organizations or institutions within the local govern­ ment. Public services play an essential role in resolving social problems (Theodorakopoulos, S � anchez Preciado, and Bennett 2012 ), environmental protection (Tress, Tress, and Fry 2006 ), and grand challenges (Whittington and Yakis-Douglas 2020 ), especially by bringing together stake­ holders (Ackermann, Pyrko, and Hill 2023 ) and enhancing collaborative knowledge creation (Mauser et al. 2013 ). Conversely, local governments face problems in activating their regions and struggle to gather various people (Armitage, Marschke, and Plummer 2008 ). Moreover, to consider a public plan that deals with the transfer of skills and knowledge, we identified the municipal meister institution as a research site. This study examined the municipal meister institutions established to facilitate the demonstration, announcement, and transfer of high-level skills. While conducting this research, each institution was considered as a single case study (Yin 1994 ), and cases were compared to determine the factors leading to success and fail­ ure. In this study, 22 municipal meister institutions were identified ( Table 1 ). However, some institutions no longer operate. This study focuses on municipal meister institutions, because their institutional frameworks are compatible with the definitions of CoPs. First, it has the three elements of a CoP: domain, community, and practice, as defined by Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder ( 2002 ).

sections.text: 33 The second is an institution of skill transfer embedded in society. Municipal meister institu­ tions connect skilled workers scattered throughout the local communities. Third, municipal meister institutions surpassed company boundaries. Although the primary purpose of the corporate meister program is to pass on skills within the company, the municipal meister program, which certifies and allows technicians to work beyond the boundaries of the company, promotes interactions between people inside and outside the company within the CoP. Fourth, the municipal meister institution affects not only technicians, but also the public, and its structure is similar to that of a transdisciplinary CoP. Moreover, the municipal meister institu­ tion is appropriate as a case study related to the TDCoP because it has multiple objectives: it involves local technicians in a CoP, engages them in skill-transfer activities, and educates local people about their skills. However, based on the classification provided by Tress, Tress, and Fry ( 2006 ), a municipal meister institution is not a “perfect” TDCoP because skilled workers and local people do not work together based on a common goal. Nevertheless, from the perspective of the local govern­ ment-administering institutions, TDCoPs can be considered for two purposes. In this study, the activities of each municipal meister institution—skill transfer and raising hands-on awareness— were also topics of focus. By focusing on these activities, the formation of TDCoPs was examined.

sections.text: situation of the institution and why has it stopped? The answer to this question provides valuable data for comparison with other cases. For local governments with municipal meister institutions, we conducted interviews in two stages: the first stage with public officers and the second stage with municipal meisters who had a high level of knowledge and skills. First, we interviewed officials who coordinated with the Meister institution. Our interview guidelines concerned institutions and CoPs. The former includes the history of the institution, recent activities of meisters, and rules for selecting and adapting candidates as meisters. The latter concerns whether they have any community and the function, effectiveness, or activity of the CoP. Each interview lasted approximately one hour and the author recorded and transcribed the data. Documents regarding these institutions were also obtained. After the interviews, we asked them to participate in the next stage of the investigation, an interview with individual municipal meisters. All local governments allowed this, and we asked interviewees who behaved positively as meisters. Based on these recommendations, we inter­ viewed 2–10 meisters per municipality. Some meisters did not want to be involved in their activ­ ities, but we obtained data from them through interviews with civil servants. In the second stage, we interviewed meister craftsmen in each municipality. We interviewed the participants in their factories, studios, and homes. Before and after the interviews, we obtained general explanations about their work, skills, practice, and actual products at their work­ place. The interview guidelines covered their careers, jobs, history of becoming highly skilled craftsmen, the process by which they became municipal meisters, and their activities as meisters. If they were involved in CoP activities, we asked them about their activities and why they were involved in CoPs. We observed their skills and developed an understanding of their work. Meisters often lecture others on their work and skills, so their explanations are clear. The inter­ views lasted about an hour or an hour and a half in Japanese and were recorded. The author transcribed and translated the data. Occasionally, documents or products were obtained from craftsmen. There are two opportunities for further investigation of CoPs. First, we observed a CoP learn­ ing activity conducted by Kitakyushu meister institute. In the event, welding skills and knowledge were lectured on, and we observed how the meister taught their skills and knowledge, and how other craftsmen learned and interacted with each other. During the observations, we took field notes (Emerson, Fretz, and Shaw 2011 ) for recording and reflection. Second, we conducted par­ ticipatory observations during the experiential event of producing a product conducted by the Niigata meister institute. During the experiential event, we often stopped creating and observing the other participants’ work and the meister’s instructions. After the event, we asked questions and took field notes for recording and reflection. Relevant documents were collected from each institution during the interviews. We then observed skills related to the skill-transfer activities in which the meisters were involved. In some of the meister programs, participants were able to observe the actual teaching circumstances. In one case, the Niigata meister program provided an opportunity for the public to participate as students in skill-training activities. A total of 49 interviews were conducted in 22 municipalities. The data collected were used to construct the case studies ( Table 2 ). Subsequently, four comparative case studies were conducted. As will be explained later in this paper, we compared the municipalities in which the institution continued and selected four meis­ ter institutions as successful. We considered whether each institution was successful by checking whether they achieve

sections.heading: Municipal meister institutions
sections.text: The word “meister” is derived from a social institution in Germany (Deissinger 2015 ) and is used as a title for high-skilled artisans who have amassed significant experience, skills, and knowledge in a certain job. In the spirit of respecting their skills, Japan has two institutions that bear the name “meister”: corporate and municipal meister institutions. The corporate meister institutions were established based on the companies to promote the transmission of skills within the com­ pany and improve the status of technicians in terms of compensation. Certified craftsmen are appointed as trainers for their successors. Japanese policies for skilled workers have centered on awards from the national government, industry associations, and unions. Advanced skills have been handed down exclusively through on-the-job training at companies, as well as through for­ mal and informal apprenticeships between employees. However, there is not much of a system in Japan to evaluate skills acquired through on-the-job training. Therefore, corporate meister institu­ tions are used as internal grading systems for evaluating craftsmen. Local government offices implemented municipal meister institutions to identify local high- level artisans. There were three reasons for the establishment of municipal meister institutions. The first is improving the social status of skilled workers and their industries. The second reason, related to the first reason, is to improve the degree of recognition of skills-based jobs in their regions. The third and most important reason is the transfer of high-level knowledge and skills to others, especially to young workers. Table 2. List of interviewees. sections.text: In general, the process of authorizing meisters is as follows. First, the local government recruits candidates for the meister program, and these candidates can also be recommended by industrial associations. The candidates are examined by a committee before being pronounced meisters. The candidate age plays a key role in adjudication. Meisters must present their intentions to engage in various activities that the committee also considers. Once a candidate was deemed wor­ thy of the title, they were admitted to the institution and pronounced as meisters at the ceremony. Many municipalities find it difficult to locate candidates for meister programs, and their deci­ sions are based on recommendations from industry associations and unions. Although it is pref­ erable to certify them annually, it is not always possible to identify candidates. As shown in Table 1 , some municipalities certified a small number of meisters over several years. However, it is not always necessary to certify the meisters annually. As will be discussed later, meisters are required to engage in certain activities, and without their cooperation, it is difficult to activate an institu­ tion. Municipalities with fewer certifications selected cooperative meisters carefully. Moreover, a difference was observed in the number of certified meisters among municipalities that was pro­ portional to the population and size of the municipalities. For most local governments, the implementation and continuation of these institutions have proven difficult, as they must include both artisans and non-artisans (residents). Although educat­ ing residents and students about the importance of skills is an important task, it is also necessary to conduct skill transfer activities for artisan groups. The latter, in particular, is not adequately promoted in many municipalities despite its importance. However, it is difficult to enhance arti­ sans’ skills because they experience various boundaries. However, it is challenging to involve non- artisans, as most of this group typically lacks interest in acquiring manufacturing skills. Moreover, some local governments have trouble finding suitable candidates for the meister pro­ gram each year. Owing to these obstacles, some municipalities’ meister institutions are moribund, whereas other local government offices continued to identify the best method to implement their municipal meister programs. However, some municipalities successfully implemented these programs. These institutions are currently operating and have implemented a process of knowledge and skill transfer between arti­ sans. To preempt this conclusion, municipalities that have achieved the objectives of the meister institution, namely, passing on skills to groups of craftspeople and educating locals, have estab­ lished a transdisciplinary CoP with the meister at the center. Four cases of the successful estab­ lishment of CoPs are presented. In the following section, we introduce the content of the institution and explain the discussion points of the TDCoP and TBOs.

sections.heading: The Kobe meister institution: organizing meisters transdisciplinarily
sections.text: Kobe meister institution is one of the most traditional institutions and highly influential among municipalities. It was established in 1993 and continues to admit meisters. Kobe meister admits meisters from service industries, primarily because it presents appropriate post-admission activ­ ities for meisters and because of Kobe’s industrial nature. Kobe meister institution dispatches meisters to schools as special lecturers, as students in the area are more familiar with and inter­ ested in service industries than manufacturing industries, which also explains Kobe Meister’s con­ tinued operations and success. The Kobe meister program admits young meisters and elevates them as successors. Each younger meister was paired with an older, more seasoned artisan in the same area to enable effective knowledge and skill transfer. Highly skilled meisters are often older adults, and even after being certified, they quickly lose their ability to participate in lectures and other activities because of their age. This type of succession system will help create a continuous connection between meisters and residents.

sections.heading: INTERNATIONAL STUDIES OF MANAGEMENT & ORGANIZATION
sections.text: 37 Kobe meister is very active because of the benefits it offers to certified meisters. The local gov­ ernment provides financial support to promote the skill-awareness activities of the meisters, pro­ viding an incentive for them to engage in these activities. Additionally, the Kobe meister certification can be used to promote companies. For example, a meister certified in confectionery can demonstrate the quality of a product by displaying this certification. This had a major influ­ ence on the Kobe meister institution. One of the unique features of the Kobe meister institution is the autonomous formation of a community of meisters. Meisters in many municipalities are from different industries; thus, they are rarely organized. However, the Kobe meisters formed a community that transcended industry boundaries and met regularly. Kobe meisters organize themselves into groups that meet spontan­ eously and even travel together. Although these meetings are only conducted for recreational pur­ poses and do not facilitate mutual knowledge creation, they seem to be effective in fostering relationships, thus allowing meisters to exchange ideas on how to effectively present lectures to their students. At Kobe meister, the TDCoP was built by highly skilled meisters from various industrial areas. In addition, Kobe meisters have been engaged in teaching their skills and knowledge to the pub­ lic, especially to schoolchildren. In other words, the Kobe meisters built CoPs among craftsmen in an interdisciplinary manner and partly involved the public. Kobe City could partly build a TDCOP because, first, craftsmen prefer to communicate with each other rather than share know­ ledge and skills. It is difficult to exchange skills across industries; therefore, they first establish friendships and then gradually exchange opinions or philosophies. This procedure is effective for building a TDCoP. In TBO, the meisters often use products to explain their skills and knowledge. They introduced themselves as citizens of Kobe. They live and work in Kobe, where some meis­ ters own shops. Representing a city can create familiarity that acts as a TBO for learning purposes.

sections.heading: The Hamamatsu meister institution: brokering knowledge through meisters
sections.text: Compared to other institutions, the Hamamatsu meister is relatively new. However, since their establishment in 2010, meisters have been admitted without interruption. The institution admits meisters from manufacturing industries and highly values seamless knowledge and skill transfers. In Hamamatsu, the meister, who voluntarily gathers participants and builds a CoP, is at the core of the program. Many Hamamatsu meisters own manufacturing companies and using their own teaching facilities is more efficient. For example, a meister conducts camp-style group train­ ing for skill transfers at his company’s training facility (an old Japanese house). The participants were often young successors of the company and technicians were interested in passing on their skills. Local company managers nurture their successors by participating in the meisters’ skill transfer activities. In addition to passing on skills, young successors can share their experiences as managers in the manufacturing industry and pass on their knowledge and experience to run future companies. Networking among successors also provides valuable opportunities to engage in dialogue from similar perspectives. Hamamatsu meister company managers also accepted successors from other companies as interns to gain work experience. Although this practice of mutual acceptance is not a part of the meister’s institution, it has traditionally been implemented by acquaintances. In addition to train­ ing successors in their own company, successors can greatly improve their skills by gaining experience in other companies and building networks outside their own company. By linking this system with the meister institution, young successors from companies that do not know each other can receive guidance more easily. Many young successors participate as interns under the supervision of meisters, and a network of successors can be established through their work. This leads to the creation of a system that jointly receives large orders that cannot be fulfilled by the 38

sections.heading: Y. MATSUMOTO
sections.text: company alone. The program also contributes to the creation of an ecosystem of small and medium-sized enterprises. At the Hamamatsu meister, the CoP was established among meister craftsmen in the manufac­ turing industry. In addition, the meister craftsmen conducted a collective training event for young successors. This means that Hamamatsu meisters built CoPs interdisciplinarily among regional companies (low transdisciplinarity) and involved young local residents (successors) in transferring skills and knowledge. The city of Hamamatsu was able to partially build a TDCoP because the meister craftsmen pursued a common benefit: cooperative training of successors. They can easily interact with each other because they are all in the manufacturing industry, but they said they needed to make efforts to interact with the younger generations. To help them, they used an old Japanese house as a TBO for group training. Similar to outdoor schools, using an appropriate learning environment is effective for learning and mutual understanding, and enhances trans­ formative learning.

sections.heading: The Kitakyushu meister institution: Nurturing transdisciplinary CoPs
sections.text: The Kitakyushu meister was established in 2001. Kitakyushu City has long been a manufacturing city, operating a meister institution for craftsmen in the manufacturing industry only (it currently operates other certification systems for the service industry). Kitakyushu has always engaged spe­ cial lecturers at technical and junior high school levels to assist students. However, the city later considered implementing programs to foster high-level knowledge and skill transfer. Consequently, they organized the “Kitakyushu meister Takumi-juku” (meaning “special lectures by meister technicians” in Japanese). With this special program, the Kitakyushu meister suc­ ceeded in passing on skills through the meister institution, which other municipalities were unable to do successfully. For several reasons, the special lecture “Takumi-juku” became one of the most successful aspects of the meister Program. First, the special lecture program has experienced an influx of participants, as recommended by different companies annually. Second, the program is highly specialized and focuses only on the transfer of selected manufacturing knowledge and skills such as welding or lathing. Third, the lecturers were involved in both academic and practical lectures. Meister lecturers convey and transfer their knowledge and skills through practice, which is also the most interesting and engaging experience for participants. Fourth, co-sponsoring the program with the Vocational Ability Development Promotion Center in the city proved to be effective. This center succeeded in helping the meister focus on teaching. The author attended a special welding lecture, during which a typical training day was observed. The welding meister begins the lecture by demonstrating his skills and knowledge through a series of complex material manipulations and fabrications. Subsequently, the partici­ pants were asked questions about welding to which the lecturer responded by providing further demonstrations. Artisans gathered around the meisters to observe their skills. Some students brought in materials used in actual work that they were experiencing problems with at their com­ panies and asked questions such as, “I want to weld this part in this way, but I cannot do it.” In response, the meister solved the problem by performing it in front of the person rather than explaining it verbally. Sometimes meisters encounter new and stimulating methods. Meisters are eager to teach, based on the motives of “I want my skills to be passed on to many others” and “I want my students to leave with as much joy as possible because they are serious about the sub­ ject.” Rather than an one-way passing-on of skills, students motivate each other through interac­ tions in a learning environment. One factor motivating participants was their desire to encounter people involved in the same line of work. The excellence of Takumi-juku lies in its ability to form a CoP, in which people who share the same awareness of issues gather to discuss common problems and share skills and

sections.heading: INTERNATIONAL STUDIES OF MANAGEMENT & ORGANIZATION
sections.text: 39 knowledge. Similar to a sectional meeting at an academic conference, participants can experience being in a “group of people doing the same job” that they cannot experience at their own com­ pany. The joy of having fellow technicians share the same technicians and have the ability to talk to each other is fully understandable. It is also stimulating for meisters as they encounter methods from various companies, sometimes even new to them. Local governments are making efforts to establish environments that facilitate the creation of networks among technicians. To generate conversations among technicians, the participants took time to eat lunch at the same table. The technicians were most excited to discuss their work dur­ ing breaks while chatting about cigarettes. For technicians in small and medium-sized companies, there may be only a few technicians in the same trade, or sometimes only one. Unable to surpass the skills of their seniors or learn other skills. However, through contact with people from other companies in the same line of work in Takumi-juku, they can gain different types of stimulation. The lecture session was followed by a casual gathering during which the artisans could interact and form career-building relationships with each other and their meister lecturers over a meal. During this gathering, the artisans and the meister shared further knowledge about welding, and the participants invited the meister to their companies for knowledge sharing. Similarly, there are events in which companies seek the guidance of a meister welder to help their technicians become certified. The meisters teach the young technicians welding skills, exchange contact infor­ mation, and establish relationships in which they can consult each other if they have any ques­ tions. Kitakyushu meisters are a source of knowledge for local technicians and the CoP, which can build such relationships, plays an important role. At the Kitakyushu meister institution, the CoP was established among manufacturing crafts­ men who continued to share skills and knowledge. On another occasion, meisters held training sessions for younger craftsmen and lectures for schoolchildren. This means that the Kitakyushu meisters built the TDCoP by establishing CoPs in an interdisciplinary manner among craftsmen and involving the general public as younger people. The city was able to build TDCoP because, first, the meisters conducted both the special “Takumi-juku” lecture event and the lecture for young craftsmen separately. This allowed each event to be held at an appropriate level, which was effective for both the events. Second, the meisters considered events as valuable networking opportunities. By recognizing these events not only for learning but also for networking, the craftsmen were motivated to participate. Through TBO, meisters can use their results. Transformative learning was used to demonstrate this procedure. Moreover, networking events have transformed the craftsmen’s beliefs from those of an isolated person to those of a community.

sections.heading: Niigata meister: including the public in the meister program
sections.text: The Niigata meister is a municipal meister in Niigata Prefecture. It was established in 2005 to certify highly skilled craftspeople, primarily located in central Niigata Prefecture, and to promote local industry and the transmission of skills by conducting activities to pass on skills. The primary target group comprised skilled craftspeople engaged in traditional crafts. The Niigata meister Institution is actively used to pass on skills in traditional crafts, and skills instruction in high schools is spreading throughout the prefecture. Niigata meisters operates the Niigata meister School to pass on skills and promote an under­ standing of traditional crafts. Although this activity, wherein meisters pass on their skills, also provides training for corporate technicians in the form of skills, such as turning and inspection, an important feature of the program is that it creates opportunities for the general public and students to experience the skills of meisters and the joy of manufacturing. This provides an opportunity for the public to take advantage of the relatively easy-to-apply nature of traditional crafts. The author had the opportunity participated in a hands-on engraving course. Three 40

sections.heading: Y. MATSUMOTO
sections.text: participants were instructed by a meister carver on how to make a leaf brooch manually before final processing. This task was simple and easy to perform. Many attempts have been made to make it easier for the public to perform these tasks. The most important factor to keep in mind is to be careful not to injure one’s hand at the edge of the copper plate. However, based on their experiences, it was evident that the meisters were paying attention as they wore gloves and ensured that the materials were firmly secured. Characteristic instructions in the preparation of assignments allowed participants to complete the assignments themselves. Meisters often showed examples but did not modify participants’ assignments. The meister did not try to control everything, but watched the students as they worked freely, paying attention only to safety and the finished product. For example, a student who finished early attempted to make another leaf brooch from a leftover copper plate. The instructor did not seem to criticize him. He taught students the depth of their skills while encour­ aging their creativity. After the work is completed, the meister collects the finished pieces and sends them to the students. The students were satisfied with their work and asked questions about other pieces that the meisters had created through hand engraving. Meister also said that he hoped to deepen the society’s understanding of engraving by participating in this type of activity. Niigata meister School is a noteworthy example of a local government meeting that builds relationships with the residents based on their skills. By utilizing the advantages of the handicrafts industry and actively providing skills instruction to the public, the municipal meister institution can directly and visibly contribute to fostering respect for their skills and revitalizing the local community, which is the main purpose of the institution. At the Niigata meister, a CoP was established between residents and meisters during special experiential lectures. However, these activities were sporadic in each individual. This means that they tried to establish relationships with residents but found it difficult to build as TDCoP. First, they require a mutually stable connection among the CoP meisters. They belonged to each craft area, but needed to cross their boundaries. However, meisters can create a boundary cross among the public. They effectively used their products as TBOs and conducted school events to enhance the citizens’ ability to cross boundaries. If craftsmen build stable CoPs, they can convert them into TDCoP.

sections.heading: Discussion
sections.text: In this study, an exploratory study was conducted—from the perspective that TDCoPs and trans­ formative boundary objects facilitate transdisciplinary boundary crossing and knowledge shar­ ing—to address the question of how TDCoPs are formed and how TBOs bring about transformative learning. To this end, we discuss how TDCoPs succeeded using four successful cases from municipal meister institutions.

sections.heading: How municipal meister institutions succeed as CoPs
sections.text: As shown in Figure 1 , 22 municipal meisters from each local government are examined. Unfortunately, most institutions failed or closed; they could not continue activating themselves. There are several possible reasons for this inactivation. First, failed institutions were unable to continuously gather candidates for the meister pro­ grams. Except in big cities such as Tokyo, the population of artisans who are candidates for meis­ tering is limited. Most local governments depend on industrial groups to search for candidates. However, in successful institutions, government officers took the initiative to search for candi­ dates; consequently, they could continue to authorize new mediators for decades. For municipal meister institutions, such as CoPs, meisters are core members who play an important role in

sections.heading: INTERNATIONAL STUDIES OF MANAGEMENT & ORGANIZATION
sections.text: 41 progressing activities and gathering other members. However, the number of meisters could not be increased automatically, which is why local government officers needed to find candidates such as Kitakyushu meisters. In Kitakyushu, city officers struggled not only to find candidates for the meister position but also to persuade candidates who hesitated to become meisters. Our cases show that the coordinator of a TDCoP plays an important role in scouting core members. When gathering members for CoPs transdisciplinarily, members often cannot access the networks of other disciplines; in other words, they do not know the people in other disciplines. In the case of municipal meisters, for example, artisans in the service industry do not know people in the man­ ufacturing industry, and vice versa. Even in the manufacturing industry, lathe artisans often do not know wire rope artisans and welder artisans do not know mold artisans. Cundill, Roux, and Parker ( 2015 ) focus on implementing TDCoPs rather than gathering members. Previous research on COPs has focused on networking skills (e.g., Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder 2002 ) and has assumed that gathering members depends on spontaneity based on interest. It should not be assumed that transdisciplinary members come voluntarily from different disciplines. Therefore, the scouting activity of the TDCoP coordinator is important. Second, it was necessary to create interactions between the meisters. Most institutions that failed could not make mutual connections between the meisters, from which they were isolated. Previous research focused on the interactions among the members because of their similar inter­ ests. However, it is difficult for TDCoP members to interact with each discipline. Conversely, suc­ cessful municipal managers can interact with local governments. For example, Kobe meister interacts with meisters by organizing groups and conducting travel activities. They could engage in personal interactions that were distant from each artisan’s work discipline, and mutually com­ municate their professionalism. Similarly, interactions between meisters across generations may have occurred in Kobe. Young meisters can learn from older meisters by succeeding in opportu­ nities, not only about their activities but also about their work and skills. Similar learning oppor­ tunities across generations were created in the Hamamatsu meister, and craftspeople educated younger successors at manufacturing companies. Furthermore, in Kitakyushu, the meister visited companies with younger craftspeople to edu­ cate them on their invitations. Based on these cases, we claim that it is easier to create interaction opportunities across generations and personal relationships. Thus, developing these interactions into transdisciplinary ones with actual problem-solving activities would be beneficial. Third, successful municipal meisters used TBOs to induce transformative learning among par­ ticipants, dramatically changing their values and perspectives. In Kobe, meisters influence other members’ perspectives through interactions among the meisters. Meister communication groups played a role in facilitate transformative learning as TBOs. In Kitakyushu, Takumi-juku (special lectures by meister technicians) worked as TBOs to transform their perspectives and enable inter­ action among the artisans. Therefore, the artisans began to interact, learn, and communicate. Moreover, the meister provided concrete career goals for the participants. Communication and interaction with meisters at Takumi-juku enhance transformative learning. Using meisters as TBOs to change the values or perspectives of members and participants is effective in activating other local governments.

sections.heading: To build TDCoP or progress CoPs for complete TDCoPs
sections.text: Next, we considered how to build TDCoP or advance CoPs for full TDCoPs, and how to use TBO for comparison with the four case studies of municipal meister institutions. Cundill, Roux, and Parker ( 2015 ) suggested three lessons for fostering TDCoP but did not suggest a specific way to build one. We found some implications for the case studies. First, compared to Niigata, which first involved the general public, and Hamamatsu, which built a mutual understanding among meisters before involving the general public, it was clear that building relationships among core 42

sections.heading: Y. MATSUMOTO
sections.text: members or professionals was preferred. Gathering nonacademic people or the general public to pursue transdisciplinarity is essential; however, doing so without relationships among core mem­ bers may lead to negative results or limited outcomes. A “relationship first, involvement later” approach would be appropriate. Similar to Kitakyushu, both the activities should be performed separately. Second, in comparison with Kobe, where the meister CoPs were built heterogeneously across industries, and Kitakyushu, where the craftsmen CoPs were built homogeneously within occupa­ tions such as welding or lashing, we suggest an interaction. In Kobe, the interactions of meisters were limited to professionalism, such as philosophy or education, and the building of personal relationships. It was difficult to achieve a deep interaction because of the differences in occupa­ tions. When choosing an interaction that focuses on mutual understanding and professionalism, they build a good relationship that allows them to share how to engage in the various activities of the meisters. However, in Kitakyushu, they interact without limits and at a practical level, such as solving actual problems, welding products, and lashing materials. Practical interaction leads to good relationships within the same occupational group, and we should choose two types of inter­ action appropriately based on whether CoP members are homogeneous or heterogeneous. Third, we consider how to involve disinterested people in each community. In our case study, it was necessary to involve the residents in cooperative activities. Local governments have imple­ mented measures to guide TDCoP development. Most local governments send meisters as lec­ turers in schools. These lectures aim to improve students’ skills and knowledge; however, this approach is ineffective because it is a one-way lecture that does not involve students in further activities. By contrast, successful institutions engage in more interesting activities. In Niigata, some meis­ ters attend lectures for residents on how to use their skills. These practical and hands-on events enabled participants to change their values regarding their skills and craftsmanship. In Hamamatsu, meisters took on young successors and trained them for a long time. Sufficient time is needed to change members’ values and perspectives and involve them in TDCoPs. In Kitakyushu, the meisters worked to educate the younger generation to pass on their own skills, not only in Takumi-juku, but also in lectures on qualification examinations. In previous research, TDCoPs required collaboration between academic and nonacademic participants. However, it is difficult for the residents to participate in these activities. In the case of munici­ pal meister institutions, there were various non-technical participants, including not only resi­ dents such as citizens and students, but also young technicians, successors, and government officials. Young technicians, in particular, are important as “semi-technical participants” in bridg­ ing the gap between meister technicians and local residents. We propose that the role of “semi- technical participants” is crucial for uniting the members of TDCoPs in several steps. We believe that our suggestions will be effective for building TDCoPs or developing CoPs for TDCoPs.

sections.heading: How to use TBO for transformative learning
sections.text: We also consider the use of TBO for transformative learning. We claimed that using TBO to make people change their stereotypes and prejudices and involve disinterested people in CoP activities was effective to use TBO. However, the research on TBO is limited and constructive. We address this problem by reviewing four case studies. In previous studies, the examples of TBO were actual data related to teaching content (Tsurusaki et al. 2013 ), wild animals and natural plants to be protected in the environment (Sato, Pemba, and Nakagawa 2018 ), and the lakes in danger of disappearing (Matsumoto, Kasamatsu, and Sakakibara 2022 ), all examples were materials and entities. Whereas, TBO in the case studies were meisters and their group (Kobe), group training in an old Japanese house (Hamamatsu),

sections.heading: INTERNATIONAL STUDIES OF MANAGEMENT & ORGANIZATION
sections.text: 43 meisters and their event “Takumi-juku” (Kitakyushu), meisters and their event “meisters school” (Niigata), that is, all meisters themselves and their activities or events. Therefore, it is unnecessary for TBOs to be materials or entities. Considering CoPs and TDCoPs, if the core members and their activities are TBOs, it would be useful to use them, at least in the beginning, to demonstrate them. This might lead to transformative learning and develop concerns about and interest in par­ ticipating in TDCoPs. How can TBOs be effectively used? We may have obtained ideas from the case studies. First, we divide CoP events without concern. In the case of Kitakyushu, the craftsmen were surprised that there were many people in the same profession in their city, which made them interested in other people. Newcomers are often forced to participate by their companies, which bring them to events such as TBOs. Coercion can be useful in creating opportunities. The second goal is to nurture a TBO guide for transformative learning. In Niigata, meisters serve as deliberate guides for introducing experiences to the public. In Hamamatsu, meisters guided young successors in their professions through group training. Meisters, as TBOs, can act as leaders to guide disinterested people toward transformative learning while conducting events. However, in Kitakyushu, civil servants act as guides by supporting the events of the meisters. They facilitated participants’ understanding of skills and knowledge, built relationships with each other, and helped newcomers with little interest. The important point in using TBO is not only to prepare it, but also to visualize it.

sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.text: We introduced the necessity of enhancing boundary crossing of “disinterested people” in CoPs for continuous learning activities and complex problem solving. In addition to previous research on CoPs and boundary crossing, we reviewed the TDR, which investigates the involvement of stakeholders in problem-solving knowledge creation. We then argued for building transdiscipli­ nary communities of practice (TDCoPs) to encourage different participants to cross boundaries and use transformative boundary objects (TBOs) to change the stereotypes and prejudices of dis­ interested people who have new concerns and interests for participating in TDCoPs. To address these issues, we conducted a case study of local authorities’ TDCoPs. We searched for 22 municipalities in which such institutions existed and selected four success­ ful municipalities for the construction of case studies. All the cases built CoPs to improve know­ ledge transfer and attempted to involve local residents and craftspeople in their events. We identified the success points of institutions that built CoPs and TDCoPs, advanced relationships among craftsmen, used TBO to bring transformative learning to participants, and provided effect­ ive support to public officials. We also examined methods to build TDCoPs, develop CoPs for TDCoPs, and use TBO. For TDCoPs, we suggest prioritizing core member relationships over citi­ zen participation, considering CoP types to build relationships, and using semi-technical partici­ pants as bridges for participation. Regarding TBO, we suggest forcing disinterested individuals to participate in events to maintain guidance and improve their understanding of TBO.

sections.heading: Theoretical and practical implications
sections.text: The theoretical contributions of this study are as follows. First, we propose concrete aspects required to establish and manage TDCoPs. Previous studies have highlighted the important role of solving complex problems, such as environmental problems, and have discussed how to build CoPs; however, their ideas are still abstract and cannot provide suggestions on how to establish TDCoPs (Cundill, Roux, and Parker 2015 ). This study addresses this problem, and we have built the theoretical foundation for TDCoPs. To continue the discussion on how to involve different stakeholders, the building and management of TDCoPs can be improved to solve complex prob­ lems by using TDCoPs. We also demonstrate the possibility of developing research on CoPs. 44

sections.heading: Y. MATSUMOTO
sections.text: Previous research has only focused on members who have interests (Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder 2002 ), and further research is required to consider disinterested people as CoP members. Second, we use TDR to discuss how people are involved. Previous research has claimed the importance of involving stakeholders from different disciplines, but has also discussed the meth­ ods of implementing this. This is especially true for grand challenges involving environmental and sustainability issues. Considerable research has been conducted in this area, its usefulness is evident. The use of TDR as a framework for complex problems, as well as TDCoPs, could be use­ ful in research. Transdisciplinarity must be considered in terms of collaborative knowledge cre­ ation and sharing. This research has already been done (Mauser et al. 2013 ), but further research is needed in the management field. Third, we identify individuals of disinterest as important can­ didates for future CoPs. Previous studies have ignored these individuals as “outsiders,” but they can become future members to contribute to the ongoing activities of the CoP. We also consider non-interested stakeholders as candidates for working together to resolve problems. In the case of municipal meisters, residents have become members of CoPs, as well as craftsmen. We should deal with disinterested individuals as local human resources for TDCoPs and discuss methods of doing so. Finally, we discuss the useful functions of TBOs. Previous research has highlighted the importance of gathering and involving these people; however, little research has been conducted on how to involve them. To involve people who are not interested in solving complex problems, it is necessary to change their values or perspectives. Academic researchers are left behind when engaging in ongoing activities. Transformative learning with TBOs can keep the participants engaged. Discussion on this topic has begun (Matsumoto, Kasamatsu, and Sakakibara 2022 ), but more research is needed. There are also four practical implications of this study: First, focus on “outsiders” to build TDCoPs as well as interested participants. Disinterested people must be considered as candidates for future membership. Addressing these concerns and interests is more important than simply waiting for them. This point also needs to be addressed by the members of interest. Their con­ cerns or interests often change or renew (Wenger, McDermott, and Snyder 2002 ), which can make them disinterested. The core members of CoPs must always check this possibility and keep their CoPs fresh with the latest domain. This strategy eventually leads to the involvement of dis­ interested individuals. Second, the coordinator should engage in scouting multidisciplinary, inter­ disciplinary, and transdisciplinary members. This is a new task for the CoP coordinators. Instead of waiting for them, the coordinator must seek different members from different perspectives, such as academic researchers, businesspeople, government officials, and residents. In addition, coordinators should encourage interaction among different TDCoP participants, particularly by focusing on building personal relationships. We can learn how to achieve this from the case of the municipal meister, considering the relationship through mutual interaction between different disciplines (Kobe), creating opportunities for members to interact in formal and informal situa­ tions (Kitakyushu), cooperative training of successors (Hamamatsu), and practical experience in learning skills (Niigata). Third, the coordinator should manage members in a transdisciplinary manner to address heterogeneity as an useful feature of activities. It is useful to build TDCoPs to manage this, and transdisciplinary interactions among different members can be an effective source of learning and innovation. sections.heading: Limitations and future research directions
sections.text: This study has two limitations. First, not all our cases were “perfect” TDCoPs, and they were still under construction. There are some limitations in discussing TDCoPs; however, we can explore some of their aspects. Second, we could not explore the reasons for this failure in detail. Most failures were due to the size of the municipality, and we could interview public officers but not individual meisters. Third, this study was exploratory and did not collect quantitative data; we could investigate the number of meisters and establish the year and type of institution based on website data. The next step was the quantitative research. Finally, we have been researching meis­ ter institutions intermittently for several years. However, owing to COVID-19, the research had to be stopped for a long time, which delayed it. There are four areas for future research are as follows: First, we wanted to develop a theory for TDCoPs, particularly regarding the way they are developed and managed. In this paper, we proposed ideas for developing an ideal model for the construction of TDCoPs. To this end, more cases of different TDCoPs need to be studied, not only for learning and knowledge transfer but also for problem solving. Second, we intend to develop a theory of TBO and show the importance of using TBO, but more research is needed to deepen our understanding of how to find, use, and create TBO. Similarly, different TBO examples of TBOs to investigate transformative learning in TDCoPs. We assumed that there are appropriate methods for identifying and using TBOs for each objective. Third, further research on the leadership of TDCoP coordinators is required. In our study, we clarified the role of the staff who coordinate meister institutions. This is useful for managing TDCoPs continuously; likewise, we need to discuss the leadership of the coordinator, especially when gathering members at the beginning. The coordinator’s leadership is essential for managing different stakeholders and improving the creation of useful knowledge (Wenger- Trayner and Wenger-Trayner 2021 ). Further research is required in this area. Fourth, the role of residents must be discussed. In the Niigata meister Institution, citizens participated in the activ­ ities, but more effort was needed to continue the activities. Spontaneous and continuous partici­ pation in TDCoPs is crucial for the success of further activities and problem-solving. Therefore, a system must be developed to implement this. Further research is required in this area.
